q: King John seals the Magna Carta at Runnymede.
w: Runnymede, June 1215 — the king first put his seal under the law. He ignored it within weeks.

q: The Black Death reaches Europe aboard Genoese merchant ships.
w: Autumn 1347, at Messina — within five years perhaps a third of the continent was gone.

q: Gutenberg prints his 42-line Bible, the first major book made with movable type.
w: Mainz, around 1455 — about 180 copies, and Europe was never private again.

q: Columbus makes landfall in the Americas.
w: October 12, 1492 — an island in the Bahamas he insisted on calling the Indies.

q: Leonardo da Vinci begins painting the Mona Lisa.
w: Florence, about 1503 — he carried it with him for the rest of his life.

q: Martin Luther posts his Ninety-five Theses.
w: Wittenberg, October 1517 — the split that remade Europe began as a complaint about indulgences.

q: William Shakespeare is born in Stratford-upon-Avon.
w: April 1564 — his actual birthday is unknown; the record is his baptism.

q: The Gunpowder Plot is foiled and Guy Fawkes is captured.
w: November 5, 1605 — thirty-six barrels of gunpowder under Parliament.

q: Newton publishes the Principia Mathematica.
w: 1687, paid for out of Edmond Halley’s own pocket — the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

q: Peter the Great founds St. Petersburg.
w: May 1703 — a new capital raised from a swamp, by imperial decree.

q: The Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.
w: Philadelphia, July 4, 1776 — news crossed the Atlantic by sailing ship, weeks later.

q: Parisians storm the Bastille.
w: July 14, 1789 — seven prisoners freed, one revolution begun.

q: The United States concludes the Louisiana Purchase.
w: 1803 — 828,000 square miles from Napoleon for about four cents an acre.

q: Napoleon is defeated at Waterloo.
w: June 18, 1815 — four days later he abdicated; the exile to Saint Helena followed.

q: The Stockton & Darlington opens as the first public steam railway.
w: September 1825 — Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first fare-paying passengers.

q: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species.
w: November 1859 — the first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on day one.

q: The American Civil War begins at Fort Sumter.
w: April 1861 — the bombardment lasted a day and a half; the war lasted four years.

q: The Suez Canal opens to shipping.
w: November 1869 — it cut the London-to-Bombay run by thousands of miles.

q: Alexander Graham Bell is granted the telephone patent.
w: March 1876 — the same day he made the famous call to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here."

q: The Eiffel Tower opens as the entrance arch to a world’s fair.
w: March 1889 — critics called it a "useless and monstrous" tower. It was meant to come down in 1909.

q: The first modern Olympic Games open in Athens.
w: April 1896 — 14 nations, no women athletes, and a marathon winner who became a Greek national hero.

q: The Wright brothers make the first powered airplane flight.
w: December 17, 1903 — four flights at Kitty Hawk; the longest lasted 59 seconds.

q: Ford introduces the Model T.
w: October 1908 — "any color so long as it is black" came later; the price kept falling instead.

q: The RMS Titanic sinks on her maiden voyage.
w: April 15, 1912 — over 1,500 died in water just below freezing. The Californian never answered.

q: The First World War begins.
w: July–August 1914 — a Sarajevo assassination lit a fuse the whole alliance system had laid.

q: The 19th Amendment is ratified, giving American women the vote.
w: August 1920 — 72 years after Seneca Falls, decided by one state legislator’s mother’s advice.

q: Howard Carter opens Tutankhamun’s tomb.
w: November 1922 — "wonderful things" glimpsed through a small breach by candlelight.

q: Lindbergh flies solo from New York to Paris.
w: May 1927 — 33 and a half hours, dead reckoning, and a periscope because he couldn’t see past the fuel tank.

q: Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin.
w: September 1928 — a stack of forgotten petri dishes, one careless summer, one lucky mold.

q: The Wall Street Crash wipes out the US stock market.
w: October 1929 — Black Thursday, then Black Monday, then Black Tuesday, then a decade of it.

q: The Hindenburg burns at Lakehurst, New Jersey.
w: May 6, 1937 — "Oh, the humanity!" — 97 people aboard; 62 survived.

q: The Second World War begins with the invasion of Poland.
w: September 1, 1939 — the Luftwaffe hit Wieluń at 4:40 in the morning.

q: D-Day: Allied forces land in Normandy.
w: June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history, on five beaches and from the air.

q: The first atomic bomb is tested at Trinity.
w: July 16, 1945 — "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Oppenheimer said he thought of it later.

q: The Roswell incident makes UFOs a household word.
w: July 1947 — a press release about a "flying disc," then a weather balloon, then fifty years of argument.

q: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
w: October 4, 1957 — a polished 58cm sphere that beeped at the whole world at once.

q: President John F. Kennedy is assassinated in Dallas.
w: November 22, 1963 — the Zapruder film exists because a dressmaker brought his camera to Dealey Plaza.

q: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon.
w: July 20, 1969 — Armstrong’s boot, a camera left behind to watch, and 600 million viewers.

q: ARPANET sends its first message between two computers.
w: October 29, 1969 — "LO." The intended "LOGIN" crashed the system after two letters.

q: Saigon falls and the Vietnam War ends.
w: April 30, 1975 — helicopters lifting off rooftops, the war’s most famous photograph taken from below.

q: Apple Computer is founded in a garage in Cupertino.
w: April 1, 1976 — three founders; the first product was a bare circuit board.

q: The Chernobyl reactor explodes.
w: April 26, 1986 — the announcement began with Swedish monitors noticing radiation that wasn’t theirs.

q: The Berlin Wall falls.
w: November 9, 1989 — a botched press conference and guards who stopped taking orders.

q: The Hubble Space Telescope is launched.
w: April 1990 — its first images were blurry; a 1993 servicing mission gave it glasses.

q: Nelson Mandela is elected President of South Africa.
w: May 1994 — a fully representative election, four years after leaving prison.

q: The September 11 attacks
w: September 11, 2001 — the morning the towers fell and the century found its shape.

q: The iPhone goes on sale.
w: June 29, 2007 — lines around Apple Stores; the App Store didn’t even exist until a year later.

q: The Curiosity rover lands on Mars.
w: August 6, 2012 — the seven minutes of terror, a sky-crane hover, and it stuck the landing.

q: The Fourth Crusade, diverted from Jerusalem, storms and sacks Constantinople.
w: April 1204: a crusade that never reached the Holy Land gutted Christendom’s greatest city instead, and the Venetians sailed home with its bronze horses.

q: The Peasants’ Revolt reaches London and burns the Savoy Palace.
w: June 1381: Wat Tyler’s army camped on Blackheath, burned the duke of Lancaster’s palace, and met the boy king face to face at Mile End.

q: Gutenberg is first recorded with his movable-type press at Mainz.
w: A lawsuit from 1439 had already let slip the secret press; by 1440 he was back at Mainz, and fifteen years later the Bible changed everything.

q: Galileo observes the moons of Jupiter through his telescope.
w: January 1610: four little stars that shuffled around Jupiter broke the Earth-centered sky for good. Naming them the Medicean stars was politics; the orbits were physics.

q: Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act ends slavery in most of the British Empire.
w: August 1833: Parliament voted freedom for the empire’s enslaved people, paying a vast fortune in compensation to former owners rather than to the freed.

q: Revolutions sweep Europe from Paris to Vienna in the Year of Spring.
w: Spring 1848: barricades rose in a dozen capitals and kings ran for the coast. By autumn nearly everywhere had been rolled back, but nothing was quite the same.

q: The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles, with Prussia’s king as emperor.
w: January 18, 1871: proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors while Paris lay under siege, chosen as the spot so France would never forget.

q: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat, and the Montgomery boycott begins.
w: December 1, 1955: her arrest began a 381-day boycott that carried a 26-year-old pastor named Martin Luther King Jr. onto the national stage.
